displayQuote: Don't grieve. Anything you lose comes round in another form

meta.title: Who really said "Don't grieve. Anything you lose comes round in another form"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It's a real Rumi poem — the opening of "Unmarked Boxes," Ode 1937. But the memorable English wording is Coleman Barks's 1984 free-verse rendering, not a literal translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't grieve. Anything you lose comes round in another form'?
meta.ogDescription: A genuine Rumi poem (Ode 1937) — but the famous English wording belongs to translator Coleman Barks, from 'Unmarked Boxes' (1984/1995).

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: These are the opening lines of “Unmarked Boxes,” Coleman Barks’s free-verse rendering of Rumi’s Ode 1937 from the Divan-e Shams, first published in Open Secret (1984) and reprinted in The Essential Rumi (1995). The consoling thought is genuinely Rumi’s, but the memorable English wording is Barks’s interpretation — he neither read nor spoke Persian — not a literal translation of Rumi’s words.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Open Secret (Threshold Books, 1984); repr. The Essential Rumi (1995)

source.excerpt:
Don’t grieve. Anything you lose comes round
in another form. The child weaned from mother’s milk
now drinks wine and honey mixed.
… God’s joy moves from unmarked box to unmarked box,
from cell to cell.
trail: Quote sites credit the line to Rumi with no source — Goodreads even flags that its community quotes are unverified.
The full text is the poem “Unmarked Boxes,” labelled Rumi’s Ode 1937, translated by Coleman Barks.
Independent postings confirm the poem opens with this exact line and is sourced to The Essential Rumi.
Barks “neither spoke nor read Persian… rewriting the poems based on other English translations,” so the wording is his interpretation, not Rumi’s literal words.
source.excerptNote: The famous line opens a longer meditation on loss and transformation; the whole poem, not just the first sentence, is Barks’s rendering.
source.rightsHolder: Coleman Barks & John Moyne (Open Secret, Threshold Books, 1984; The Essential Rumi, HarperCollins, 1995)
source.rightsNote: Rumi’s 13th-century Persian original is long in the public domain, but the specific English wording shown is Coleman Barks’s (with John Moyne) interpretive rendering, first published in 1984 — well after 1931 — and remains in copyright to its translators and publishers.

author.name: Rumi
author.kicker: The true author of the thought
author.heading: About Rumi
author.bio: Jalal al-Din Rumi was a 13th-century Persian poet, Islamic scholar, and Sufi mystic, born in Balkh (in present-day Afghanistan) and later settled in Konya (in present-day Turkey). His vast Divan-e Shams and the Masnavi are landmarks of Persian literature; centuries later, English “versions” by translators such as Coleman Barks made him one of the best-selling poets in the United States — and one of the most freely paraphrased.

misattribution.heading: The wording isn't quite Rumi's
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication pinned on a famous name — it is a real Rumi poem. The catch is one of translation: the line everyone shares is a 20th-century English version, not something Rumi literally wrote.

items.why: Barks is credited as the translator, but he “neither spoke nor read Persian” and reworked earlier scholarly English translations into free verse. The phrase “comes round in another form” is his, not a literal equivalent of Rumi’s Persian.

items.who: Usually cited with no source at all
items.why: Most quote sites, including Goodreads, present the line bare, without naming the poem “Unmarked Boxes,” the translator, or the book — which is why it reads as an anonymous aphorism rather than the opening of a specific poem.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the poem are genuinely Rumi’s (Ode 1937 of the Divan-e Shams); the memorable English sentence belongs to Coleman Barks, from “Unmarked Boxes.”

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: “Unmarked Boxes” is a meditation on impermanence: joy and life force move endlessly from one form to another — rainwater into flowerbed, roses up from the ground — so nothing is truly lost, only transformed. The opening line distills that whole argument into a single consolation for grief.
That is authentically Rumi’s Sufi vision. What makes the quote feel so quotable, though, is Barks’s plain, modern American cadence — the very thing scholars note can drift from the literal Persian.
context.pull: Nothing is lost — only changed in form.
